title: Data-Driven Generation of Eyes and Head Movements of a Social Robot in Multiparty Conversation

fields.value: Technical/system description and evaluation: the authors developed data-driven gaze and head-movement models, evaluated their performance, and ran an online perception study.

fields.value: Two human players collaborated in a word-scoring game while a robot animator reported themes, invited proposed words, and reported scores. Online raters judged short clips of robot behavior and gaze for relevance to context.

quotes.text: The game is scored by finding the most quoted words for a given theme (previously played online by human players).
The animator must report the themes, invites the players to propose words, and then reports the scores for the proposed words.
A sequence consists of 9 rounds (new theme word), and 5 collected answers per theme.
The evaluation instruction given to the subjects was this: “Rate the videos based on the relevance of the robot’s behavior and gaze relative to the context”.

fields.value: Objective technical measures: gaze-target classification accuracy/F1 and head-angle MSE, using nine-fold cross-validation. Subjective outcome: HEMVIP video ratings from 0 to 100; ratings were analyzed with beta regression and pairwise comparisons. A closing survey about robot familiarity and general feeling was also collected.

quotes.text: To best evaluate the performance of our models, we used the K-fold cross validation method.

On each page, the subjects compare 4 renderings of the same interaction segment. They must rate each video between 0 and 100.
At the end, they have to fill in a survey about their familiarity with the robots and their general feeling.

fields.value: The paper frames its subject as robotic gaze control and attention control in multiparty HRI, including prediction of gaze targets and generation of head movements.

quotes.text: This study introduces a unique method to control the robot gaze in a multi-party interaction by combining two Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, one to predict the attention targets of the robot, and one to generate the corresponding head movements.
In order to make the attention control of our robot as natural as possible, we propose to generate both attention targets and head movements.

fields.value: The paper describes gaze as a social cue that regulates conversation, including turn-taking and identifying the next speaker or current addressee. The proposed model predicts where the robot should direct attention based on interaction context and communication intent.

quotes.text: Indeed, in addition to transmitting emotions, it is a powerful regulator of conversations [16,27].
This function is particularly important in multiparty conversations, for turn-taking management and role detection, such as who will be the next speaker, or who is the current addressee [13,32].

Removing the Intent feature has the biggest impact on gaze prediction, which can be explained by the importance of intentions in determining whether the robot should look at the tablet (theme announcement, scores) or specific/both players (ask for proposal, validation) when speaking.

fields.value: In the online ratings, the proposed LSTM gaze control was rated as appropriate as the original behavior, but it showed no significant advantage over the heuristic control for context-aware head movement generation. The authors report no significant differences between Simulated Ground Truth and the LSTM or heuristic controls.

quotes.text: The subjective evaluation revealed that despite a moderate objective performance, the proposed control was rated as appropriate as the original behavior in the data set.

fields.value: Two cascaded LSTM models predict gaze target and head angles from multimodal inputs about robot-pilot activity and the two users; the head model also receives pilot-gaze features. Pilot gaze was classified from recorded movements, verbal features were manually annotated, and user gaze features automatically annotated. The training data came from an iCub teleoperated by a human pilot; evaluation clips were rendered on a virtual Furhat. Four control conditions were compared.

quotes.text: More precisely, we used Long Short-Term Memory networks to predict gaze target and context-aware head movements given robot’s communication intents and observed activities of its human partners.
In addition to these 17 input channels, the model generating head angles also receives pilot gaze features, adding 4 channels for a total of 21.

fields.value: The interaction corpus was collected with an iCub humanoid robot whose head and eyes were controlled via immersive teleoperation; all head and eye movements, including vergence, were reproduced in real time with 3+3 degrees of freedom. Perception clips used a virtual Furhat robot.

fields.value: The authors trained cascaded LSTM models to predict a robot animator’s gaze targets and head movements in a three-party word game. Online raters found the predicted gaze control viable, while context-aware head movement generation was not rated significantly differently from a heuristic control.

RQ1; RQ2; RQ3; RQ4; RQ5; RQ6 — The paper frames gaze as a conversational regulator, describes its role in turn-taking and addressee selection, and reports perception-rating effects. It details the sensing and LSTM control approach, identifies iCub and virtual Furhat embodiments, and discusses limitations related to third-party evaluation and physical-robot testing.
